lessons.title: How bug hunters actually work
lessons.body:
Finding web bugs is a repeatable process, not luck:
  1. MAP the app - every page, parameter, API endpoint, cookie, header. You can't test what you haven't found (use a proxy like Burp to record everything).
  2. Understand the INTENDED behavior of each feature.
  3. Then ask, at every input: what happens if I send something unexpected? Someone else's ID? A script? A URL? A quote?
Bugs live in the gap between what the developer expected and what the app actually accepts. Most of the classes below are just disciplined versions of that one question.

lessons.title: IDOR - broken object-level authorization
lessons.body:
The app trusts an ID you can change. GET /orders/1001 shows your order; what about /orders/1002? If it shows someone else's, that's an Insecure Direct Object Reference - the server authenticated you but never checked you're authorized for THAT object.
FIND: change IDs (numbers, UUIDs, filenames) and watch for other users' data.
FIX: check ownership on every object access, server-side - never trust the ID alone. (This is the single most common and lucrative bug-bounty class.)

lessons.title: XSS - cross-site scripting
lessons.body:
Your input is reflected into a page and runs as script in other users' browsers.
  Reflected: your input echoes straight back (a search box that prints your query).
  Stored:    your input is saved and shown to others (a comment, a profile name) - worse.
FIND: submit a harmless marker like a unique string, see if it lands in HTML unescaped; then test a script payload on a target you own.
FIX: output-encode everything by context, and set a Content-Security-Policy. XSS is data (your input) being treated as code (script) - the same root cause as SQL injection.

lessons.title: CSRF - cross-site request forgery
lessons.body:
A malicious page makes the victim's browser send an authenticated request to your app ('change email to attacker@evil') using the victim's cookies, without their intent.
FIND: does a state-changing request work without an unpredictable token tied to the user?
FIX: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, and re-auth for sensitive actions.

lessons.title: SSRF - server-side request forgery
lessons.body:
You get the SERVER to make a request for you. A 'fetch this URL' feature pointed at http://169.254.169.254/ (cloud metadata) or internal hosts can leak credentials or reach systems you can't touch directly.
FIND: any feature that takes a URL/host and fetches it - try internal/metadata addresses.
FIX: allow-list destinations, block internal ranges, don't let user input choose the host.

lessons.title: More classes to carry
lessons.body:
Open redirect   - /login?next=//evil.com sends users offsite; used in phishing.
  Auth/session    - weak reset tokens, no rate limiting, session fixation, JWT 'none'.
  Info disclosure - stack traces, .git/ exposed, verbose errors, secrets in JS.
  Business logic  - buy for a negative quantity, skip a payment step, race conditions.
The method never changes: map it, understand it, then push every input past what the developer expected. Report via the program's responsible-disclosure/bug-bounty process.

quiz.q: Changing /orders/1001 to /orders/1002 and seeing someone else's order is...
quiz.why: Insecure Direct Object Reference - missing object-level authorization.

quiz.q: Which bug makes the SERVER fetch an internal/metadata URL for you?
quiz.why: Server-Side Request Forgery - the server makes the request on your behalf.

quiz.q: Stored XSS is worse than reflected because...
options: it's saved and served to other users automatically
quiz.why: The payload persists and hits every viewer, not just someone you lure to a link.

quiz.q: XSS and SQL injection share what root cause?
quiz.why: Untrusted input crossing into a code/interpreter context - the data/code boundary.

quiz.q: The right first step in testing any web app is...
options: map every page, parameter and endpoint
quiz.why: You can't test what you haven't found - map the full attack surface first.
